chapters.name: The Tidal Iron
chapters.content:
The truth came to him the way plague came to Gullrot: in a fever of small signs, each one deniable, until suddenly the whole city was burning and there was no going back.

He found the first proof in the whaling ledgers — the black bindings that recorded a century of seasons. He had read them for timber records, and the wrongness surfaced like a line that did not belong: a marginal column, added in a later hand, listing the weight of each leviathan against the draft of the rendering works' hauling slips. Not tallow. Not oil. Ballast. He turned pages until his candle burned to a stub, and the same column ran through thirty years of kills, growing fatter as the years ran thin. The whalers were not hauling the deep's bodies ashore for lamp-oil. They were hauling them for the iron that caked a leviathan's bones like rust on a hull.

The maritime records were next: the charter claims, the leases the magistracy had sold for a pittance when the plague years emptied the treasury. Voss spread them on the oak table and weighted them with the tide tables, and the picture came together the way a fire does when the wind turns — not one flame but a hundred. A lease on the drowned wards, sold during the plague years for the cost of a burial. A survey of the strata beneath, marking tidal iron in the deep beds where the old river had run under the city and the tide had buried it, thick as a reef. A cross-reference to the spring thaw, when the iron would be cheap to raise. A deed of transfer, dated the year of the Sea-Cleansing, shifting the lease to the Chantry's holding — and with it, the note that the lease would expire with the leviathan season unless the land above was cleared and claimed.

He sat back. The Drowned Flats was not rot. It was a field. The people on it were a crop to be burned off before the spring plowing, and the Chantry's god was a god of balance sheets. The pamphlets condemning Mael Odrin were not theology. They were title.

Then he found the iron letter, and the last of his ignorance came down.

It was buried in a bundle of scraps kept for the weight of their seals, and among them a letter in a hand he knew from the quarantine years, addressed to a factor of the rendering works. Voss held it to the candle and read the sentence that undid him:

*The plague does the work of the fire for us. Let the quarter be named pestilent, and let the sickness be the reason, so that the iron under the drowned wards may come to the Chantry clean and unburdened by claimants.*

He read it twice, then a third time, and the third time the words were not the magistrate's at all. They were his own, in another shape. *Let the sick be gathered. Let the rot be excised.* He had written those quarantine edicts with his own hand in the plague years and believed them noble. He had drawn the fire-lines around Gullrot and called them mercy, and watched the crier announce his words from the fish-market steps, and felt the god's clean pleasure as the lever gave under his hand — and all the while, under the plague's name, there had been men like these, counting iron.

He did not move for a long time. The aerie was ringed with windows, and the whole city lay beneath him like a drawing, and he saw it now with the scales fallen: the iron vaults beneath the dry-docks, the old sluices running from them toward the Spire of Charters, the spring thaw, the expiring lease, the oil promised to the tithe's lanterns — all of it one line, drawn in commerce, signed in piety. The heretics, the smugglers, the escaped whalers with their branded shoulders: excuses. The Flats was not being cleansed. It was being culled, so that the whaling monopoly could dig down through the ashes and haul the deep's iron out of the drowned beds before any other hand could claim it.

The mirror opened under him, and he fell into it.

He had stood on the quarantine line in his leather apron, checking the geometry of the burn, and he had not seen people. He had seen a problem of fuel — structures on the fire-line, fixed points in a necessary drawing, rot to be excised. That was the horror he had carried for fifteen years, the one that outweighed even the pleasure: the subtraction that made the burning possible. And here it was again, exact and legible, in the Chantry's hand over the Flats. *Disease. Heresy. Smuggling. Rot.* Words that made the people of the quarter into a single combustible noun, so that the fire would not have to see their faces. He had written the words for Gullrot and meant them. The Chantry wrote the same words for the Flats, and the words were not a zeal — they were a price list.

He had been bought to draw a second Gullrot. That was all. Not to save Veyra, not for legacy, not for the redemptive fire that would rewrite his name. He was being asked to repeat his crime so that men who had never smelled smoke could sell iron, and the crime would be signed with his hand and blamed on his name, and the Chantry would count the weight in their ledgers and call it cleansing.

The memory came up then, the way drowned things come up when the tide turns, and it was not the lever this time. It was the writing.

He was young in the memory, sitting at a clerk's desk while the plague tore through the city outside. The crier's voice came through the shutters, hoarse and faithful, and Voss's own words came back with it: *Let the sick be gathered. Let the rot be excised.* He had written them at a magistrate's dictation, then corrected the magistrate's grammar, proud of the clean shape of the sentence. He had believed them noble — believed, with his whole mapmaker's heart, that he was drawing lines of mercy, that the plague was the enemy and the fire the cure. He had believed it so completely that when the girl with the broken doll held her toy up to his tower, he had seen a fixed point, and pulled the lever, and felt the god's pleasure, and called it duty.

He had not been lied to at Gullrot. That was the terrible part. No one had needed to sell him the lie, because he had bought it himself, with his own hand, in his own ink — the belief that some people were less than people, that their deaths were arithmetic, that the fire was mercy if the drawing was true. He had authored the dehumanizing words before the Chantry ever thought to use them, and the belief had made the burning possible. And now the Chantry had found the words waiting, already warm, and put them on over the Flats like a dead man's coat.

The shame came up out of him in a cold wave, a splash of tide across his face, and for the first time in fifteen years it was not the shame of the craving. It was the shame of the mirror. He had spent his captivity telling himself he was the man who pulled the lever — the hand, the architect. But the truth was smaller and colder: he was also the man who wrote the words that made the lever possible. He had given the fire its permission, and the girl with the broken doll had burned with a word he had written on her.

He looked at the fire plan on the oak table, nearly finished, checked nightly by the magistrate's two fingers, and he saw it for what it was: a deed. A bill of sale for a quarter full of people, drawn in his hand so that the Chantry's hands could stay clean. He was not being asked to save Veyra. He was being asked to become the Chantry's clerk of death, the man who signed the lie that let them dig the iron out of the ashes of the innocent — and if he drew it, if he pulled the lever, the lie would be his to carry forever, only this time he would carry it knowing.

The survey page was in his shoe. He took it out, and the charcoal stub with it, and sat with the page folded open and the candle burning down, reading the cross-reference to the spring thaw for the hundredth time.

He did not know yet what he would do. He knew only three things, and they stood in him like pilings driven into mud: that the Chantry's cleansing was commerce, and the heresy a name given to a thing after the useful men had finished with it; that he had written the same lie at Gullrot and believed it, and the belief had made him able to burn children; and that the fire plan on the table was not a map of the Drowned Flats at all, but a map of the Chantry's greed, drawn in their ink.

Somewhere in the small hours, with the whole city sleeping beneath the aerie's windows, Emmerich Voss began, for the first time since Gullrot, to think not about the fire's shape, but about who, in the end, deserved the burning.

The old sluices ran from the vaults toward the Spire of Charters. He had noticed that weeks ago, in another life. He looked at the plan, and then at the page in his hand, and the two drawings lay side by side on the oak table, and he did not know which hand would finish the work. But he knew, at last, that the work was a lie.

He folded the survey and put it back in his shoe. He put out the candle. In the dark, the faces came to him as they always did — the baker with his flour-dusted hands, the crier with his hoarse faithful voice, the girl with the broken doll — and with them, for the first time not in accusation but in something nearer to recognition, the living ones: Dero's steadying hand, Halla's cup of water, Sathen's offered bread, Odrin's low voice like a wave, Iskra's sharp eyes, Pella's hoarse bright laughter. The dead and the living looked at him through the dark, and Voss looked back, and he did not know yet what he would do with the knowledge in his shoe. But he knew he could not draw the fire for them. Not again. Not for iron.

chapters.name: Burning Children
chapters.content:
He dreamed of Gullrot again, but the fire had learned new faces.

The dream began as it always did: the tower, the lever, the whole quarantine quarter laid out below him like a map drawn in timber and tar. The northwest wind combed the smoke toward the water. The crier's platform stood empty at the head of the fish-market steps, its boards already warm. Below, along the line, the people waited in their thousands — the sick, the mothers, the children — and he saw them as he had taught himself to see them: as fuel, as fixed points, as the necessary arithmetic of mercy.

Then the dream turned, the way a tide turns, and the faces came up out of the crowd.

A girl near the fire-line lifted a doll whose paint flaked like ash — but it was not the doll-girl of fifteen years ago. It was Pella, hoarse and laughing, holding up her ledger like a flag of truce, and the tarred posts of the quarantine line were the fish-market steps of the Drowned Flats, and the smoke curling between them carried the salt of the quarter instead of the plague's rot. The woman who steadied a stranger's shoulder was the woman who had steadied him. The man who brought water was the man who had brought him water. And on the crier's platform stood Brother Sathen with his gray head bowed, sleeves rolled, chalk and medicine on his forearms — not crying the edicts but folding his sleeves and wading into the flame line, offering bread to the burning children one by one.

The children all had Pella's face. They had Iskra's defiant jaw. They had Sathen's kind hands and Odrin's low voice, and they burned the way the Gullrot children had burned, without noise, without struggle, because he had drawn them as fixed points first and seen them as people too late.

And the terrible part was the lever.

He stood with his hand on it — the cool iron, the give before the mechanism caught — and the god's pleasure ran up his arm like always. But this time the thrill did not arrive alone. It arrived braided with the sound of Pella calling him Cartographer across the mud flats, with the weight of Sathen's bread in his stomach, with Iskra's laughter cutting him open where any accusation would have bounced off. The pleasure and the terror were the same sensation, wound together so tightly he could not tell which end was which. He pulled the lever, and the thrill was the screaming, and the screaming was the thrill, and he woke gasping with his hand out and his mouth full of smoke that was not there.

The aerie was dark. The city lay beneath the windows, and the fire plan lay on the oak table where the magistrate's two fingers would touch it at dawn, and Voss lay on the narrow cot with his heart going like a rendering hammer, trying to remember which world he was in.

He did not light a candle. He sat in the dark and let the dream drain out of him, and when it was gone he understood, with a clarity worse than the dream, that he had been wrong about himself for fifteen years.

He had believed his punishment was the noose — the rope that never tightened, the nightly visits of the dead. It was not. The punishment was the choice.

The Chantry had laid it at his feet that first night, wrapped in piety and profit: draw the fire, pull the lever, and become the savior twice-born, the architect of a pure Veyra, the man whose name the city would carve in stone above the iron works. Legacy. The word had been warm in his hand then, the old craving purring up out of its cage. He could see the shape of that other life entire — the aerie, the maps, the adoring ledgers, the gold keeping him warm for the rest of his days. He could have it. All he had to do was repeat, knowing, the one crime that had made him.

That was the noose, he understood now. Not the rope. The offer. The Chantry had not come to punish the Butcher of Gullrot. They had come to give him a second lever, anointed, justified, profitable — and the fine line between justice and vengeance ran straight through the center of him, and he was the only man alive who could tell which side he stood on, and he had been standing on both sides for fifteen years without once choosing.

He was not innocent. That was the ground he stood on, and he would not let himself forget it. He had written the edicts. He had drawn the lines. He had pulled the lever, and the girl with the broken doll had burned because he had seen her as a fixed point, and no amount of Chantry gold would wash that from the ledger of him. He was guilty, and haunted, and the haunting was not a mistake — it was the truest thing the city had ever given him. The faces in the smoke were not accusers. They were a memory of the cost of control, and the only thing standing between the Drowned Flats and a second Gullrot.

Because the craving was still there. He had to name it, here in the dark, or he would lose the night to a lie. The craving was there, as hot as ever — the god's clean pleasure, the perfect geometry of a controlled inferno, the terrible joy of holding a whole quarter's fate in the exact center of his hand. He wanted the lever. He wanted the fire. He wanted to stand in the aerie on the night of the tithe and watch the lines he had drawn ignite exactly as drawn, and feel for one more moment the only power the world had ever let him hold. The dream had taught him that wanting did not stop at the edge of a deserving target. Wanting was a tide; it rose for iron and for mercy alike.

But the tide, Sathen had said, carries whoever will be carried. And he had known, since the bread, since the chapel, since Pella's ledger and Iskra's tunnels and Odrin's low voice like a distant wave, that he could not be carried. The deep did not ask what a man had done, only if he would be carried — and Voss was not the kind of man the deep could carry, because he was the kind who had to choose, and the choosing was the whole of it.

He got up and moved through the dark with a mapmaker's certainty to the window where the moon laid the city out in silver and shadow. The Drowned Flats lay low against the water, a scatter of lamps that were not yet fire-lines — Pella's lamp, maybe, or Iskra's, or the drowned chapel's one guttering light. Beyond them, climbing the headland, the dry-dock vaults where the accelerant would come ashore before the spring tide, and the old sluices running from them toward the pilings of the Spire of Charters, straight as a surveyor's line.

Who deserved the fire? The question that had come to him in the small hours of the ledger was still the question, but it had sharpened in the dream's wake, from a question about the Flats into a question about the ones who had drawn the lease and written the letter and called the culling a cleansing. He had spent his life aiming fire at the people power called rot. He had never once asked whose word made the rot — only obeyed it, because the words had been his own.

He was not innocent, and could not be innocent, ever again. But he could choose. That was the discovery the dream had burned into him with Pella's face: guilty and haunted, and still, in the center of all that, there was a choice, and the choice was the only thing the Chantry could not buy, the only thing the craving could not counterfeit, the only thing the noose had never touched.

The decision began to form, not as a plan — not yet, not with the magistrate's fingers on the plan at dawn and the letter in his shoe — but as a direction, a line drawn where no line had been. Not to save himself. The self was not worth saving; the self was the man who had written the edicts. To aim the blaze. To take the craving that had burned a thousand people and point it, for the first time in his life, at the architects.

He stood at the window a long time, and the city breathed beneath him, and the faces stood with him in the dark — the baker, the crier, the girl with the broken doll, and now Pella, Iskra, Sathen, Odrin, the whole living ledger of the quarter he had been bought to burn. They did not accuse him. They simply looked. But this time, instead of shrinking from their gaze, Voss looked back, and what he saw in their faces was not judgment.

It was the answer to the question. The fire was not the crime. The fire was the tool, and the crime was the aim — and for fifteen years he had aimed it where he was told, at the people the words had made rot, and called the thrill duty, and let the ecstasy of control stand in for the love of anything at all.

He did not know yet how he would do it. He knew only that the plan on the table was a lie, the letter in his shoe was the truth, the sluices ran from the vaults toward the Spire, and the spring tide was coming.

He lay down, and the faces stayed, and for the first time in fifteen years he did not try to sleep.

He waited for the dawn, and planned.

chapters.name: Rewiring the Design
chapters.content:
The woman magistrate came at dawn, as she always came, and laid two fingers on the edge of the fire plan the way another woman might touch a sleeping child's forehead.

"The alleys," she said. "You've redrawn the alleys."

"The wind changed its habits," Voss said, and the lie was smooth as tide-worn glass because it was half true. "The northwest will hold through the tithe. I've widened the eastern feeder so the smoke lays down the water and never touches the harbor." He did not look at the plan. He looked at her hand, and at the truth living under the drawing: the sluices, the vaults, the pilings, the one line drawn beneath the other until neither could be read.

The magistrate smiled. She saw the charcoal under his nails, the stoop, the tremor, the tin cup. She saw the cartographer the Chantry had bought. She did not see the letter in his shoe, or the survey, or the second map living inside him like a tide waiting for the moon.

She left. The aerie was his until nightfall.

He worked the official plan first, because the official plan was the shell that kept the truth safe. He refined it as if his life depended on its beauty — and it did. The tide-locked alleys ran east to west for the northwest wind. The tar-black mooring posts wore their small X's like a confession. The drowned chapels, the warehouses, the cellars under the fish market where the escaped whalers slept: all drawn true, all burnable, all a perfect, terrible lie. The magistrate would carry this drawing in her mind's eye on the night of the tithe and watch the lines come alive exactly as drawn.

And then, beneath it, in the small hours, he drew the other thing.

It began as arithmetic. The vaults beneath the dry-docks held the oil promised to the tithe's lanterns; the old sluices of the surveys ran from those vaults toward the pilings of the Spire of Charters, straight as a surveyor's line, and no living man had ever asked why. Voss asked. He traced them up the headland to where the Spire's foundations drank the deep stone, and the answer was waiting: a city that fears its own quarter builds itself a way to burn that quarter, and never considers that the way runs both directions.

He was not burning the quarter. That was the whole of the design. The oil would still come ashore before the spring tide; the lines would still feed the timber and climb the tar. But at every junction — a valve, a damper, a stone-cased run where accelerant could be shaped like a river shaped by a bank — he drew the rewire. Not deletions; the magistrate's eye would catch deletions. Additions that looked like refinements: a regulating sluice here, a cut-off there, a redrawn feeder carrying the oil not down into the drowned wards but up, along the old line, into the dry-dock warehouses the Chantry had filled with whalebone and rendered fat and everything a monopoly keeps close to its heart, and then on, to the pilings.

The thrill came back while he worked. It always came back — a warmth behind the breastbone, a humming in the fingers, the god's clean pleasure of a mechanism answering exactly as drawn. He let himself have it, because he had promised himself in the dark that the craving would be aimed and not denied, and aim required honesty. He watched his own hand move, precise and ecstatic, and named what he felt: power. The same power that had burned a thousand people. It was not smaller now, or kinder. It was aimed.

The memory came between one line and the next, the way it always came when he was happiest.

He was walking through the ash of Gullrot the morning after. The fires had died and the quarter lay open to the sky like a burned book, and he walked it because the architect must inspect his work. The crier's platform was a black tooth. And at the edge of the fire-line, where the flame had climbed a stall's tarred posts and eaten the awning and stopped, inexplicably, at the oven, stood the baker's stall.

The oven was still warm.

He remembered the heat on his face, and inside, untouched, a loaf — golden, risen, perfect. The bread the baker had offered him on the quarantine line, the bread he had refused because the baker was on the wrong side of the line and the line was the law and the law was him. The bread had been baking when the fire came. The fire had taken the baker and spared the bread, and Voss had stood in the ash holding the only thing the fire had left him, knowing he did not deserve to eat it.

He had put it back. He had closed the oven door. He had walked out of Gullrot and never once, in fifteen years, allowed himself to remember the weight of that loaf.

He put down the charcoal.

The loaf was not about him. It was about the baker — the kind, flour-dusted face, the hand that had fed him as a child, the bread offered across a line that should never have been drawn. The fire had left the loaf as if the universe itself had said: here is what you could have had, if you had seen the man instead of the line.

The memory became a vow. He could not undo the past — could not unbake the loaf or unburn the baker or un-ask the girl with the broken doll her name. But he could refuse to repeat it. He could see the people of the Drowned Flats and not the line. He could aim the craving at the architects, and when the fire came, the Flats would stand under a sky full of someone else's burning, and the loaf, this time, would be carried out of the oven and eaten by the people it was meant for.

He finished the rewire at dawn and hid it where the magistrate's fingers would never find it — in the numbers. The official plan was a city of fire-lines; the true design was a single arithmetic beneath it: the sluices, the valves, the pilings, the spring tide. He drew the last valve with a steady hand, and the thrill sang through him, and he let it, because this time it was bound to something it had never been bound to before.

He crossed the harbor at low tide with his tin cup and his tremor, and found Iskra Venn in the sail-loft doorway of the fish market, and told her a half-truth.

"There's a tide coming," he said. "Not the water. An upheaval. Before the tithe."

Her eyes went flat and careful, the way a captain's eyes go when a stranger knows her name. "The Chantry's cartographer. Telling me about upheavals."

"The Chantry's cartographer draws what he's paid to draw," Voss said. "And sometimes he draws the truth underneath, so that when the drawing lies, the truth survives." He let the tremor shake his hand, just a little. "The quarter is going to be moved. Not burned — moved. The tunnels under the fish market, under the chapels, under the tide: if they run the way I think, they can carry people out before the upheaval breaks."

"And if they don't run the way you think?"

"Then you'll know I'm lying," Voss said, "and you'll cut my throat in the tunnel, and the quarter will be no worse off than it was."

She laughed — the laugh that had cut him open on the market steps that first day. "You draw pictures of places you mean to burn. I know what the Chantry pays for."

"I know what they pay for too," Voss said. "I've seen their ledgers. The Flats isn't being cleansed. It's being cleared. Tidal iron, and a lease that dies with the leviathan season." He watched her face change like a tide-line when the water starts to move. "You don't have to trust me. Trust the arithmetic. The oil comes ashore before the spring tide. The fire draws its lines from the vaults. And the sluices under the dry-docks run the other way — toward the Spire. I'm asking you to have your people ready to move on the night of the tithe, and to trust the tide I tell you to ride."

Iskra studied him. Behind her, the fish market sang — a girl's hoarse bright cry, salt eel, three for a penny — and Voss did not let himself turn toward it.

"If you're lying," Iskra said finally, "I'll know before the oil does. And the tunnels will swallow you."

"That's fair," Voss said.

She gave him the map then — not on paper, but in the turns of her speech, in the places she let him see: the cellar stair under the market, the drowned chapel's sunken door, the salt-dark passage where the tide itself was a ceiling and a floor. He memorized it all with a cartographer's hunger, because this map was the other half of his own — the human chart of names and homes and stories, now joined to the stone and water that would carry them out of the fire.

Walking back across the mud flats, he felt the weight of the two maps inside him: the official lie and the true design, the fire-lines and the escape-lines, the Chantry's arithmetic and the people it was drawn over. They did not cancel each other. They were the same drawing seen from two sides — the way a valley is the same valley whether you stand in it or on the ridge above it.

The loaf was still in the oven. But this time, the oven was going to open.

The spring tide was coming, and he had eleven days to be ready, and the craving sang in him like a lit fuse, and for the first time in fifteen years he let it burn toward something worth burning for.

chapters.name: The Congregation of the Deep
chapters.content:
Iskra came to the sail-loft doorway at low tide, three days after she had given him the tunnels in speech, and Voss saw the test in the way she stood — weight on the balls of her feet, one hand loose at her hip where a knife lived.

"Walk with me," she said. "And this time, tell me where we're going before we get there."

They went down the fish market's cellar stair, past the barrels where the escaped whalers slept curled like prawns, into the salt-dark passage where the tide was ceiling and floor. She took him through twice — once fast, once slow — and at the drowned chapel's sunken door she stopped.

"Sathen," she said. "The sick can't run. So they have to be carried, and Sathen's the only man in the Flats who knows how."

"You trust him?"

"I trust he's too stubborn to let anyone die," Iskra said. "That's different from trust." She looked at him sideways. "The whole quarter has to know, or the tunnels will clog with panic and the tide will have us all."

Voss stood with water to his ankles and felt the weight of what she asked. He had drawn names, homes, stories on the hidden page; now they would be told aloud, and every word he spoke would be a lie with a truth inside it, because he could not say the truest thing: that he had come here to burn them.

He said, "The tide's coming," and that was the truth, and he let it carry the rest.

Sathen met them with sleeves rolled and forearms stained chalk and salt. "The cartographer. The drawn line. Come to tell me my chapel is on the wrong side of something again."

"It's on the side of the people in it," Voss said. "That's the side that's going to have to move."

Sathen did not ask why. He asked how many, and when, and what would carry the ones who could not walk. Voss answered in the turns of speech Iskra had taught him: the cellar stair, the sunken door, the salt-dark passage, the safe houses above the tide-line. He watched Sathen's hands move as he listened — already planning medicines, patients strapped to boards.

"You're asking me to trust a stranger."

"I'm asking you to trust the arithmetic. The quarter moves before the tithe. The only question is whether it moves in boats or in ash."

Sathen was quiet. "Odrin will need to hear this. If the congregation is to move, it must move together, or it will move in pieces and drown."

The congregation gathered that evening in the drowned chapel, and Voss stood at the back in his frayed warden's coat, watching Mael Odrin climb the little platform where a crier's platform had once stood in another quarter, another life. The tall man's voice rolled low, a distant wave.

"The city calls us rot," Odrin said. "The city writes pamphlets and calls us heresy, and we have answered by living. Now the deep asks us to live somewhere else for a while — a hard thing, an unfair thing, and true." He did not name Voss, did not point. "We will move when the water tells us, through the places the water keeps for us, and we will carry our sick and our old and our small, and we will come back when the city has burned itself out of its hatred, and we will still be here."

Voss heard the words and heard, underneath, another voice — hoarse, faithful, fifteen years dead. Let the sick be gathered. Let the rot be excised. The crier had shouted his edicts from the fish-market steps while Voss stood in the tower in his leather apron, and the words had felt like mercy, like the clean geometry of a cut made to save the body. He had written them. He had believed them noble. And here was Odrin, in the chapel the Chantry's pamphlets named rot, speaking the same shape of sentence in the service of keeping people alive instead of burning them.

The rhetoric was the same because he had authored it — the dehumanizing litany that made a quarter into a stain, a people into dross, a culling into a cleansing. The Chantry was not quoting him. They had simply learned the language at his school.

After the sermon, Voss helped. He carried boards with Sathen for the ones who could not walk. He measured the sunken door against the tide-table and told Iskra where the water would stand at the hour she meant to move her people, and she nodded, and the nod was a stone in the wall of her suspicion.

Then the girl with the ledger found him. Pella came up the mud flats with a torn net over her shoulder and planted herself in front of him. "You mend nets, cartographer? Or do you only draw them on fire plans?"

"I can mend a net."

It was true. He had mended nets as a boy on the Gullrot wharves, before he learned to draw lines around quarters. He knelt in the mud with the net across his knees and worked the twine with his steady, ruined hands, and Pella sat on an overturned cask and watched him.

"You're the one telling everyone to move. Where to?"

"Away. To the high ground, the safe houses, the tunnels. And back, when it's over."

Pella's bare feet swung. "The day I leave, it should be because I want to, not because some stooped man says a tide's coming."

"The tide's coming whether I say it or not," Voss said. "The only question is whether you're standing on the right side of the wall when it does."

She was quiet, and he mended, and the net came together under his hands — the same rhythm as drawing a line, the same satisfaction of a thing made whole, and entirely different, because what was made whole was not a plan but a tool for keeping a girl alive.

"Sathen says you eat bread," Pella said. "He says you're not entirely made of ink and smoke."

"Sathen talks too much."

"He also says the deep doesn't ask what a man has done." She looked at him, ten and a half years old and older than the tide-wall. "What did you do, cartographer?"

The question sat in the mud between them. Voss could feel the whole truth in his mouth — the tower, the lever, the girl with the broken doll — and could feel it would not fit, that it would break the bright careful ledger of her world if he said it here.

"I drew lines," he said. "I drew lines around places, and believed the lines were mercy."

Pella nodded slowly, as if that made sense. "The net's done. You can have salt bread with us tonight, for the mending."

They ate on the tide-wall as the dark came in — salt bread and fish broth, Pella's family, the fish-sellers, the children who played among the salt-scoured bones, Sathen, and Iskra with her back to the wall and her eyes on the harbor. Voss sat among them in his frayed coat, tin cup in hand, and the bread was coarse and good, and the people passed it to him without counting the cost, and he knew he did not deserve a single crumb.

That was the worst of it, and the best: not that they thanked him, but that they did not need to — they fed him the way the tide feeds the shore, without keeping a ledger. They would be ash without his intervention; he knew it, and they did not, and the knowledge sat in him like the weight of the untouched loaf he had put back in the baker's oven fifteen years ago. He made himself eat anyway, because refusing the bread this time would be the same sin as refusing it then.

The crier's voice returned that night as he lay on sailcloth in the chapel, listening to the water breathe against the sunken door. Let the sick be gathered. Let the rot be excised. The Chantry's pamphlets over the Flats were the same words in a new hand, and the congregation of the deep were the ones the city still meant to excise.

He was not that hand anymore. He had aimed the craving at the architects, and the aim had grown teeth and a plan. But the language was his and would always be his, and the only thing he could do with it now was refuse to let it win — stand in the chapel, mend nets, carry boards, eat bread he did not deserve, and make sure that when the fire came, it was the city's ledgers that burned and not the people they were written over.

In the dark, from somewhere on the mud flats, he heard Pella practicing her cry for the morning — salt eel, three for a penny — and the sound of it was like the tide coming in, and he let it wash over him, and did not refuse it.

Eleven days had become nine. The chapel knew. The market knew. The congregation knew. The whole quarter was learning to move, and the craving sang in him, and for the first time in fifteen years it sang in time with the voices instead of over them.

chapters.name: The Spring Tithe
chapters.content:
The night of the Spring Leviathan tithe arrived dressed in its own oil.

Every lamp in Veyra burned the Chantry's promise. Lanterns strung from the Mercy Spire to the harbor wall, oil-banners snapping green and gold above the quays, fat-wax candles guttering in ten thousand windows—the city had poured its storehouses of light onto the water until the harbor lay like a second sky, and the Drowned Flats beyond it lay dark, low, patient, waiting to be lit. Voss stood at the barred window of the aerie and watched the festival and thought: the whole city is burning their oil and calling it a celebration. The oil that came ashore before the spring tide. The oil that was to have fed the fire-lines of his plan.

Behind him, the woman magistrate folded her hands. "The northwest wind is up," she said, "and the tide is right. The quarter has never been so still. They must feel it coming."

Voss did not answer. Across the harbor, the lamps of the Flats were going out one by one, in a pattern no one above would read as an evacuation—the fish market dark first, then the drowned end of the east-west alleys, then the tide-wall, the last small lights winking down out of sight as Iskra's people took the cellar stair, the sunken door, the salt-dark passage where the tide itself was ceiling and floor. He had given her the water-hour in arithmetic, and she had nodded, and he trusted that nod more than he trusted anything the Chantry had ever promised him. The last light he watched was one small flame moving along the wall and down, and he imagined Pella carrying it, her hoarse voice hushed for once, and he let himself believe she was already under the stone.

"Come," the woman magistrate said. "They want you at the vaults before the signal."

They took him down through the Spire—the ledger-keeper with the brass key, the two oil-dark captains, the rowers—out through the water-gate and along the foot of the headland, where the dry-dock warehouses loomed black and full of whalebone and rendered fat and everything a monopoly keeps close to its heart. The vaults breathed oil from their stone mouths. The ledger-keeper unlocked the iron door of the gallery with his brass key, and Voss stepped inside, and there it was, waiting for him in the lamplight like a thing that had never stopped waiting:

A lever. Cool iron, worn smooth at the grip, the same weight, the same faint give before the mechanism caught. The same kind of lever he had pulled fifteen years ago, from the tower above Gullrot, while the crier's hoarse faithful voice announced the decrees he had written—Let the sick be gathered. Let the rot be excised.—and the girl with the broken doll stood at the quarantine line holding up her flaking-paint doll toward the tower, as if the man at the lever might see a child and hesitate. He had not hesitated. He had pulled, and the lever had given, and the thrill had been the sweetest thing he had ever held, and he had stood in the tower and believed the rot was real and the excision was mercy.

The thrill was here now. Hotter than ever, singing up his arm from the iron before he even touched it, whispering of legacy and control and a city rebuilt in his image—the architect Veyra needed once more, the man who had burned away the plague and would burn away the stain, savior twice-born. He let himself feel it, because feeling it was the only honest thing left. He named it for what it was: the god's clean pleasure of a mechanism answering exactly as drawn. Fifteen years, and it had not dimmed. It had only been waiting for a worthy target.

Above them, in the aerie, they would be gathering now—the whaling magnates, the maritime magistrates, the ones who had read the iron letter aloud to themselves and smiled at the phrase The plague does the work of the fire for us. They would pour their tithe-wine and watch through the ring of windows for the spectacle of righteous fire, for the proof that commerce wears piety's mask and wins. They expected the Drowned Flats to bloom below them like a hell-garden, the heretics, the smugglers, the escaped whalers with their branded shoulders, the whole quarter reduced to ash so the tidal iron beneath the mud could be raised unclaimed by the spring thaw. They expected him to be their lever.

Voss laid his hand on the iron. It was warm, as if the years had kept it in a fist. The thrill climbed his wrist, up the old familiar channel to his chest, and for one long, suspended moment he stood exactly as he had stood above Gullrot, exactly as he had stood the second before he pulled and became the Butcher of Gullrot forever.

The baker's face floated up out of the smoke of memory—kind, flour-dusted, the hand held out with bread on the quarantine line, the name he had called as the stall's tarred posts caught. The loaf, untouched, warm in the oven the morning after, the weight of it he had never allowed himself to remember, until he had walked it back into this very night as a vow. The crier's voice, cut off mid-syllable, swallowed by the roar. The girl with the broken doll, her paint flaking like ash, the question she had never gotten to ask. And Pella, hoarse and laughing at the tide-wall, salt eel three for a penny, watching him mend her net with the eyes of someone who has not yet learned which strangers to fear. Iskra, watching him through stone and suspicion, waiting for him to be exactly what the Chantry had made him, ready to cut his throat in the dark if he proved it true. Sathen's kind hands. Odrin's low voice. The salt bread eaten on the tide-wall with people who did not know they had been marked with an X.

Behind him, the ledger-keeper said something about the signal, about the lantern lifted at the aerie window, about the moment when the northwest wind would carry the smoke over the water and spare the harbor. Voss heard the words as he had heard the quarantine edicts he once wrote—noble, reasonable, signed in commerce and called piety.

He thought of the ledgers. The tidal iron strata beneath the drowned wards. The lease expiring with the leviathan season. The deed transferring the lease to the Chantry in the year of the Sea-Cleansing. The iron letter folded in his shoe, still warm against his ankle: the culling is commerce.

The lever waited. The thrill waited, and he did not deny it—he could feel the whole drawn geometry of the night in his fingertips, every regulating sluice, every cut-off, every valve hidden in the numbers that looked like refinements, and the map of it was beautiful, and it was his.

He chose.

The hand that had hovered came down. The mechanism gave, smooth as it had given in Gullrot, and the thrill broke over him like a wave of godlight, the same terrible pleasure, hotter and cleaner than it had ever been, because this time he knew exactly what he was doing. This time the fire had been drawn with love.

Down in the stone gut of the vaults, the oil left the galleries and ran along the old sluices, and instead of falling into the drowned wards where the last lamps had already gone out, it climbed the headland, black and obedient, feeding the feeding-lines he had redrawn beneath the Chantry's own feet. The first flame took in the dry-dock warehouses, where the whalebone and rendered fat and everything a monopoly keeps close to its heart had been stacked for the fire that was meant to fall elsewhere. The second flame took the tar-black mooring posts of the Chantry's own quay. And the third took the foundational pilings of the Spire of Charters, rising through the old timber like a judgment climbing stairs.

From the aerie above, a window bloomed orange. Then another. In the gallery of the vaults, the woman magistrate's voice rose and cracked, calling the design wrong, calling him traitor, and Voss turned from the lever with the thrill still singing in his chest and looked up through the smoke at the Spire he had drawn to burn, and at the dark, quiet, emptied Flats beyond the harbor, where not one lamp was left to catch, because the people had already gone down under the stone, carrying their sick and their old and their small, carrying a mended net and a hoarse bright voice, into the salt-dark passage where the tide itself was ceiling and floor.

The fire rose. It was beautiful, terrible, and just, and Voss stood in the middle of it, on both sides of the fine line, and let it take the first of the night's answers off his hands.

chapters.name: The Flipped Design
chapters.content:
The design flipped in the space of a heartbeat, and Voss felt it in his teeth before he saw it with his eyes.

He had drawn this geometry a hundred times in his mind — in the aerie at night with the charcoal stub and the hidden second map, in the tunnels under the Flats with Iskra's turns of speech running through him like a tide-table. Now the mechanism had given, and the whole shape of it was running through the stone like a pulse. The oil had left the vault galleries. It had not fallen into the drowned wards where the last lamp had already gone out. It had climbed the headland instead, obedient to the regulating sluices and cut-offs and the one valve hidden in the numbers that looked like refinements, and it was feeding the fire beneath the Chantry's own feet.

The first flame took the dry-dock warehouses. Voss felt it as a change in the air pressure around him, a sudden warmth through the stone, and then the groan of burning whalebone as the rendered fat caught. The second flame took the Chantry's own quay, the tar-black mooring posts he had walked past disguised as a broken warden. The third took the foundational pilings of the Spire of Charters, rising through the old timber like a judgment climbing stairs.

Behind him, the woman magistrate's voice rose and cracked. "The design runs wrong. It runs—" and then, as the first orange bloom broke through a window of the Spire above them, "traitor."

Voss turned from the lever. The thrill was still singing in his chest, hotter and cleaner than it had ever been at Gullrot, because this time he knew exactly what he had drawn. He looked up through the smoke at the fire rising exactly where he had planned it, and he felt the old god-pleasure run through him one last full measure before something else moved in behind it.

He named it. He had spent fifteen years refusing to name anything, but he named this: the thrill was real, and it was his, and it was aimed.

"Traitor," the magistrate said again, and her voice was small now, a flag going down in a wind. She took a step toward him, and then the stone floor shuddered, a crack ran up the gallery wall, and a sheet of burning oil poured through it like a second tide. The captains were shouting. The ledger-keeper with the brass key was scrabbling at the iron door, and the door was hot, and the key was turning in his shaking hand, and beyond it the vaults were already a furnace of the Chantry's own oil.

Voss looked at the woman who had inspected his charcoal-smudged fingers for loyalty, who had read the fire plan with her lips moving as if she were praying, who had stood in the aerie and called the cleansing a spectacle of righteous fire. She was not praying now. She was watching her world come apart, and somewhere in the reflection of the flames in her eyes Voss saw the girl with the broken doll again, the baker's flour-dusted face, the crier's throat cut off mid-syllable, and he understood with a strange, quiet clarity that he was looking at the difference between the two fires.

At Gullrot he had stood above the people and believed the rot was real and the excision was mercy. He had felt the thrill then, too, and let it stand unexamined, and the faces in the smoke had come for him every night for fifteen years. Tonight the thrill had a target he had chosen, and the faces in the smoke were not the ones he had burned. They were the ones he had carried out.

The iron door gave. The ledger-keeper stumbled through it into the burning corridor, and the magistrate followed, her composure gone, her fine coat smoldering at the hem. Voss stood at the lever a moment longer, because he wanted to feel the weight of the choice on purpose, the way a man holds a coin he has decided to spend.

Above him, the Spire of Charters was burning from the foundations. He could hear it through the stone, a deep chewing sound as the old pilings gave, and he could picture the aerie exactly: the long oak table where he had drawn the beautiful lie for the magistrate's dawn inspections, the ring of windows where the whaling magnates and maritime magistrates had gathered with their tithe-wine to watch the Drowned Flats bloom like a hell-garden. They were watching their own world bloom instead. Somewhere up there a window shattered, a ledger page curled to ash, and the iron letter's authors discovered that the plague does the work of the fire for us cuts both ways.

Voss turned his back on the lever and followed the heat of the doorway.

The corridor was a throat full of smoke. The captains had gone ahead, or gone down; he could not tell. The magistrate was bent double before him, and the ledger-keeper ahead of her, and the way out was a pale rectangle of night where the water-gate opened onto the foot of the headland. Voss moved through the smoke with the map of the vaults fixed in his mind — he had drawn this building in the first days of his captivity, marking every load-bearing wall and tar-soaked post with an X, and the knowledge had never left him. He knew where the fire would run before it ran, which corridor would hold its air longest, which lintel would fall last, which way the tide would come in under the water-gate when the pilings gave.

Behind him, the Spire shuddered, and a sound like a great beast settling came down through the stone, and Voss thought of the aerie windows going orange one by one and the tribunal watching their own reflection in the glass.

He did not weep. He had not wept since Gullrot, and he would not start tonight, because weeping would be a mercy to himself and he had decided he was not owed any. But as he came out through the water-gate onto the strip of quay, the night air hit his face like cold water, and he stood a moment and looked back.

The Spire of Charters stood against the burning sky like a black ribcage holding a heart of flame. The dry-dock warehouses were gone, their whalebone and rendered fat feeding a fire that roared like the sea. The Chantry's own quay burned along its whole length, the tar-black mooring posts flaring like candles set out for the dead. The headland was a single drawn line of fire, exactly as he had charted it, beautiful and terrible and just.

And beyond it, across the dark harbor, the Drowned Flats lay untouched.

The low roofs, the tide-wall, the drowned chapel sunk half a story into the mud, the fish-market steps where Pella had stolen his notebook, the salt-dark passage where the tide itself was ceiling and floor — all of it dark, all of it empty, because the lamps had gone out in evacuation order and the people had gone down under the stone, carrying their sick and their old and their small, and the fire had nothing there to feed on. Where the Chantry had expected a hell-garden to bloom, there was only the patient dark of a quarter that had moved itself out of the way of a fire that was not meant for it.

Voss stood on the quay and let the thrill spend itself through him like the last of a fever. It had been the sweetest thing he had ever held, at Gullrot and again tonight, and he did not pretend it had changed. But it was tempered now, the way a blade is tempered — heated and struck and cooled — and what it had been aimed at made all the difference. He had not become a hero. The faces in the smoke would still come for him; he would carry the girl with the broken doll and the baker's untouched loaf and the crier's silenced throat for the rest of his life, and he deserved to. But he had become something he had not been in fifteen years: a man who chose the direction of his own burning.

He was a just arsonist. He stood on both sides of the fine line between justice and vengeance, and the line ran straight through the middle of him, and he had drawn it there himself, in flame.

The magistrate came out of the water-gate behind him, dragging the ledger-keeper, whose brass key had burned a brand into his palm. She saw Voss standing at the edge of the quay, his face lit by the fire he had set, and for a moment her hatred and her terror fought each other across her features.

"You," she said. "You drew our death."

"I drew your design," Voss said. "You told me where the fire should go. I only corrected the aim."

"The whole city will hang you."

"Let them," Voss said. "I was hanged fifteen years ago and the noose never tightened. I have been dead a long time. Tonight I found something worth being dead for."

He did not wait for her answer. He turned his back on the burning headland and walked along the quay to the place where the wall dropped to the water, where he knew — from a smuggler's turns of speech, from a tunnel map memorized in arithmetic — that a certain loose stone gave onto a stair leading down to the cellar under the fish market, and from there into the salt-dark passage, and from there to the people carrying a mended net and a hoarse bright voice through the stone, waiting for the water-hour, waiting for the man who had promised them a tide of upheaval he would control.

Behind him the Spire of Charters fell in on itself with a sound like a name being crossed out, and the fire of the flipped design climbed to meet the burning sky, and Voss did not look back. He had looked back once, at the lever, and seen what he needed to see. The rest of the night belonged to the living.

He had drawn the fire with love, and it had gone where he drew it, and now he was walking through the stone after it, into the dark where the people he had saved were waiting to learn exactly who had saved them — and he did not know whether that learning would be a second fire or a third chance. It did not matter. The direction had been chosen, and a man who has chosen can walk through anything.

The loose stone gave. The stair went down. Voss took the first step into the dark, and the fire of the Chantry's own design burned on behind him, exactly as drawn, exactly as just, exactly as terrible — and over the water, where the last of the Flats' lamps had gone down under the stone, the first gray seam of the approaching dawn began to show against the burning sky.

set.name: Emmerich Voss
set.description: Condemned mass murderer, the Ignition Man, the Butcher of Gullrot; now a just arsonist standing on both sides of the line between justice and vengeance. Location: on the quay at the foot of the burning headland, having just escaped the ignition gallery and vaults through the burning corridor and water-gate as the Spire of Charters collapsed; he has begun descending through the loose stone at the quay wall (from Iskra's tunnel map) down toward the cellar stair under the fish market and the salt-dark passage, to rejoin the evacuation before the water-hour. Still disguised as a broken former warden. Physical/emotional condition: the old god-thrill broke over him hotter than ever at the lever but is now spent and tempered; he consciously named it and accepted it is his, aimed at a target he chose; he did not weep, refuses self-mercy, and told the magistrate 'I have been dead a long time. Tonight I found something worth being dead for.' Goal: descend through the tunnels, reach the survivors before the water-hour, and face the moment when they learn who he is and what he drew.

set.name: Chantry of the Deep Ledger
set.description: Secret tribunal of whaling magnates and maritime magistrates. Location: the Spire of Charters, which has now fallen in on itself from the burning pilings; the dry-dock warehouses and the Chantry's own quay are ash; the aerie and its ring of windows where the tribunal gathered with tithe-wine were consumed, and with them the ledgers, the tidal-iron lease, and the iron letter's authors — the plague does the work of the fire for us cut both ways. set.name: Iskra Venn
set.description: Smuggler captain of the Drowned Flats, tall, coarse salt-and-black hair in a rope, tarred coat over fisherman's jersey; stands with weight on the balls of her feet. Location: leading the evacuation through her tunnels beneath the Flats on tithe night — the cellar stair under the fish market, the salt-dark passage where the tide is ceiling and floor, the drowned chapel's sunken door — toward the safe houses above the tide-line, at the water-hour Voss gave her in tide-table arithmetic. State: she trusted his nod-arithmetic and moved the quarter; she still does not know he is the burn-man or that the fire falling on the Chantry's headland is his design; her throat-cutting threat stands unresolved if she learns the lie, but she is carrying the people out exactly as the half-truth demanded. Goal: get the whole quarter through the tunnels and above the tide-line while the city burns.

set.name: Mael Odrin
set.description: Preacher of the congregation of the deep, tall and weathered, voice a low roll like a distant wave. Location: moving the congregation out through the tunnels on tithe night as he preached they would — carrying the sick, the old, and the small, keeping them together so they move as one people or none. State: he preached the move as survival and did not name the cartographer; above them the city is burning in the wrong place; he does not yet know Voss is the burn-man. Goal: hold the congregation together and bring them above the tide-line alive.

As the Spire of Charters collapsed above him, Voss escaped the ignition gallery and burning vaults through the smoke-filled corridor and the water-gate onto the quay at the foot of the headland, moving with the vaults' fire geometry fixed in his mind; he did not look back until he had seen the fire exactly as drawn — warehouses, quay, pilings — and the Drowned Flats dark and untouched across the harbor.

The Spire of Charters fell in on itself with a sound like a name being crossed out; the aerie and its ring of windows where the tribunal gathered with tithe-wine were consumed, and with them the Chantry's ledgers, the tidal-iron lease, and the iron letter's authors — their own accelerant completing the culling of the cullers.

The woman magistrate and the ledger-keeper survived the vaults, dragging each other out through the water-gate onto the quay; the brass key burned a brand into the ledger-keeper's palm. The magistrate accused Voss to his face — 'You drew our death' — and swore the whole city will hang him; Voss answered that he corrected the aim of their own design and that he had been dead a long time and found something worth being dead for. Her pursuit remains live.

On the quay, with the thrill spent and tempered like a blade, Voss consciously named what he had become: not a hero — the faces in the smoke will still come for him and he deserves them — but a just arsonist, a man who chose the direction of his own burning, standing on both sides of the fine line between justice and vengeance and drawn there in flame.

Across the dark harbor the Drowned Flats lay untouched — low roofs, tide-wall, drowned chapel, fish-market steps, salt-dark passage all dark and emptied, the lamps gone out in evacuation order and the people under the stone; where the Chantry expected a hell-garden to bloom there was only the patient dark of a quarter that had moved itself out of the way of a fire not meant for it.

At the quay wall Voss found the loose stone he knew from Iskra's tunnel map, gave onto a stair down to the cellar under the fish market and the salt-dark passage beyond, and took the first step into the dark to rejoin the evacuation before the water-hour, leaving the collapsed Spire burning behind him as the first gray seam of dawn showed against the sky.

Voss is descending the loose-stone stair into the tunnels beneath the fish market to rejoin Iskra's evacuation; he must reach the column of survivors moving toward the safe houses above the tide-line before the water-hour, and the reunion will be where the full truth of who he is can no longer be hidden.

chapters.name: Through the Tunnels
chapters.content:
The stair went down in darkness so absolute the stone seemed to breathe it. Voss counted the steps the way Iskra had taught him in turns of speech — seventeen to the landing where the wall sweats, then the turn, then thirty-one more where the water's voice comes up through the floor. His hand rode the wall like a blind man's. Above him, through the stone, the Spire of Charters groaned and settled and went on burning, a great beast dying by inches.

He had mapped this passage for escape while pretending to map it for fire. The thought followed him down the steps like an old companion: the same tunnels he had charted as fire-lines — the tar-soaked mooring posts, the timber foundations, the cellars where escaped whalers slept — had become, in the end, the lines of their salvation. The lie and the truth had shared the same ink.

At the bottom the salt-dark passage opened, and the tide's voice came up through the floor, and a small light moved in the dark ahead, and a hoarse voice he knew said, "There you are."

Pella stood with the flame cupped in a lantern of pierced tin. Her mended net was over her shoulder, her ledger in her belt, her face smudged with soot she had not earned. Behind her the column of the quarter stretched away into the dark — Sathen's sick on boards carried by the congregation, Odrin's low voice passing the word back like a wave, the old and the small moving as one people or none.

"You're late, cartographer," Pella said.

"The arithmetic held. I'm on time."

"You're shaking."

He looked down at his hands. They were shaking — the god-thrill spent, but the body still remembering the lever, the give of the mechanism, the heat climbing the headland. "It's the smoke."

Pella's eyes narrowed. She had stolen his notebook once and read it aloud at the tide-wall, and she had asked him what he did, and he had told her he drew lines and believed them mercy.

"You smell of burning," she said, "and you weren't under the stone with the rest of us. Where were you, cartographer, when the city caught fire on the wrong side of the water?"

The column had stopped. Voss felt the whole length of it turn toward him in the dark, felt a hundred held breaths. Then Iskra's voice came up the passage, flat and tarred.

"That's what I'd like to know too."

She came out of the dark like a ship out of fog, and she was looking at him the way she had on the first day in the sail-loft doorway, when she had seen through the broken-warden disguise and mocked the burn-man to his face. But there was something else in her eyes now, something counting.

"The Spire is burning," she said. "The warehouses. The Chantry's own quay. And you walk out of the stone smelling of it, on the hour you gave me in tide-table arithmetic, and I find I'm not surprised." She took a step closer. "Tell me what you drew, cartographer. Tell me the whole lie this time, or I'll keep the promise I made you in the sail-loft."

The truth sat in his throat like a stone — the name, the fifteen years, the lever pulled twice, the second map hidden in his shoe beside the iron letter. He had rehearsed this moment through the burning corridor and the water-gate and the loose stone, and there was no shape to the words that would not sound like an excuse.

Pella got there first.

"You're him," she said. Not loud. The lantern shook in her hand, her shadow thrown huge against the sweating wall. "You're the burn-man. You came to burn my home. You stood on my tide-wall and ate my mother's salt bread and mended my net, and you were going to burn us."

The silence in the passage was absolute. Even the tide seemed to hold its voice.

"Yes," Voss said. The word came out clean and finished, the first true thing he had said about himself in fifteen years. "That's who I am."

He waited for Iskra's blade, for the congregation to close around him the way it had closed around a stranger on the day of the chase, this time to tear him apart. He deserved that. He had decided he was owed no mercy, and now the bill was presented.

Pella did not raise her voice, and she did not raise the lantern. She stepped forward and took his hand.

It broke something in him that the fire and the lever and the magistrate's curse had failed to break — not weeping, nothing so kind, but the hard shell of the fifteen years, cracked along a single clean line. Her hand was small and warm and calloused from hauling nets, and it held his with a certainty that asked nothing.

"Iskra said the deep doesn't ask what a man has done," Pella said. "Only if he will be carried. You carried us. Now you get carried."

Behind her, Iskra's knife had not come out. She stood a long moment, reading him, then gave a single nod — the same nod that had been the first stone of trust in the wall of her suspicion — and turned back up the passage.

"Move," she said. "The water-hour doesn't wait for confessions."

The column moved, Pella's hand in his, and as they went the sound of the burning headland came down through the stone — not pursuit, but its opposite. The fire was cutting the Chantry's enforcers off from the quay, sealing the water-gate behind them with a curtain of flame, buying the dark quarter the only coin it had ever owned: time. Weapon and shield, and he had aimed it so that every edge faced the men who would have come with swords and brands, every flat of it lay against the people who moved beneath his hand.

Somewhere behind them a muffled roar went up — the vaults giving way, the last of the Chantry's oil feeding its own pyre — and Voss thought of the tower at Gullrot.

The memory came complete, the way they all came, with the smell of cold iron and the city laid out below like a map drawn in lamplight. He had stood at the lever and known. He had known the crier's platform stood on the fire-line, known the girl with the broken doll was holding it up toward his window, known the baker's stall at the edge of the line would take the first climbing tongue of flame. And he had known he could warn them. That was the part he had buried deepest: a bell-rope within reach, a horn, a voice of his own that could have carried. He had stood there with the warning in his throat and the lever in his hand, and he had chosen to watch.

He had chosen to watch, and the watching had been the pleasure, the god's pleasure, the part he had never confessed to any court.

The girl's hand tightened in his.

"The passage floods ahead," Pella said. "Iskra says you know where the water will stand."

Voss came back to the salt-dark passage, to the tide's voice rising through the floor, to the wet stone and the carried sick and the old woman borne past him on Odrin's back. The tower at Gullrot receded into the dark behind them, unreachable, unchangeable. He could not undo that choice. The memory would come for him every night for the rest of his life, and he would deserve it every night.

But this fire was still being chosen, step by step, in the dark, by a man who had finally stopped watching.

"The water will stand to the third lintel at the sunken door," he said, and his voice was steadier than he had any right to expect. "We pass the sick through first, over the boards. The chapel stair keeps its air above the line. Tell Iskra I'll take the rear — I know which stone holds and which stone turns."

Pella ran the words forward. Somewhere ahead, Iskra's laugh came back down the passage, short and incredulous and almost warm.

Pella returned, her hand still in his. "He says we'll be above the tide-line before the water-hour, and he says the fire keeps the Chantry's men off the quay, and he says —" She stopped, and looked up at him, and for a moment she was not the girl with the ledger but every child of the Flats he had meant to burn, and also just Pella, ten and a half, hoarse and unbroken. "He says he drew the fire so it would save us, not take us."

"He did," Voss said.

Pella considered this with the grave arithmetic of a girl who kept a ledger of prices and knew the cost of everything in the quarter. Then she gave his hand a single squeeze and kept walking.

"Then you're not the burn-man anymore," she said. "You're the one who carried us. That's what the deep will remember."

They went on through the salt-dark passage, the tide rising around the column like a patient hand, the fire of the Chantry's own design burning on behind them — weapon, shield, and at last, in the small warm grip of a child's hand, something very close to a baptism. Above them, through the stone, the first gray seam of dawn showed against the burning sky, and the people of the Drowned Flats went up out of the dark into the light, carrying their sick and their old and their small, and the burn-man walked among them and did not watch.
