set.name: Brother Sathen
set.description: Heretic physician of the Drowned Flats, small and gray-haired, sleeves rolled, forearms stained by salt, chalk, and medicine. Location: moving with the sick through Iskra's tunnels on tithe night — his patients strapped to boards carried by the congregation, his medicines carried, the ones who cannot walk carried. State: he now knows the stooped cartographer was the burn-man hired to cleanse the quarter (the confession happened in earshot of the whole column); he said nothing, and his part of the column simply kept moving. Goal: keep his sick, his branded, and his broken alive through the tunnels to the safe houses above the tide-line.

set.name: Mael Odrin
set.description: Preacher of the congregation of the deep, tall and weathered, voice a low roll like a distant wave. Location: moving the congregation out through the tunnels on tithe night, carrying the old woman on his back, passing the word back along the column like a wave. State: he heard Voss's confession that he is the burn-man and the column stopped and held its breath; Odrin said nothing, only kept the people moving as one people or none. Goal: hold the congregation together and bring them above the tide-line alive.

set.name: Pella
set.description: Scrappy fish-selling child of the Drowned Flats, about ten and a half, hoarse-voiced crier of 'Salt eel, three for a penny'; keeps a ledger of prices. Location: in the salt-dark passage with the evacuation column, carrying the flame in a pierced-tin lantern, her mended net over her shoulder and her ledger in her belt, walking hand in hand with Voss toward the sunken door and the safe houses. State: she learned who he is — she named him the burn-man ('You came to burn my home... you were going to burn us') and he confessed; she did not forgive him, but she took his hand and kept running. She told him 'the deep doesn't ask what a man has done, only if he will be carried,' that he carried them so now he gets carried, and that he is no longer the burn-man but the one who carried them, which is what the deep will remember. Goal: stay on the right side of the wall when the tide comes, and keep hold of the burn-man's hand until they are above the tide-line.

In the salt-dark passage beneath the Flats, Pella named Voss the burn-man who came to burn her home; Voss confessed plainly: 'Yes. That's who I am.' Iskra heard it, kept her knife sheathed, gave her single trust-nod, and ordered the column to move; the full truth is now known to the whole evacuation column.

Instead of forgiving or condemning him, Pella took Voss's hand and kept walking; she told him the deep does not ask what a man has done, only if he will be carried, and that he is now the one who carried them. Her gesture cracked the hard shell of his fifteen years along one clean line without bringing weeping.

In the tunnels Voss confronted the final Gullrot memory in full: in the tower he had a warning within reach — a bell-rope, a horn, a voice of his own — and chose instead to watch, and the watching was the pleasure he never confessed to any court. He accepts he cannot undo that choice and that the memory will come for him every night he deserves it.

As the column fled, the burning headland cut the Chantry's enforcers off from the quay and sealed the water-gate behind the survivors with a curtain of flame; the fire functioned as both weapon and shield, every edge toward the Chantry's men and every flat toward the people.

Voss told the column the tide will stand to the third lintel at the sunken door, the sick pass through first over the boards, the chapel stair keeps its air above the line, and he will take the rear because he knows which stone holds and which stone turns; Iskra laughed, short and incredulous and almost warm.

The evacuation column is still in the salt-dark passage ahead of the tide, moving toward the drowned chapel's sunken door and the safe houses above the tide-line; the survivors must emerge onto the rain-washed quay at dawn to face the collapse of the Spire, the magistrate's pursuit, and the question of what comes next.

The woman magistrate swore the whole city will hang Voss; her pursuit is live as the survivors emerge at dawn, and the quarter now knows Voss is the burn-man who chose their lives, which may complicate or aid his standing when the magistrate comes.
Pella has claimed Voss as 'the one who carried us'; on the quay she will ask if he will stay, and his answer (kneeling to repair the doll) will close the novel.

chapters.name: Rain on the Quay
chapters.content:
The rain began before they reached the sunken door, a thin gray hiss against the stone, and by the time the door gave under Voss's hand the whole sky had opened like a sack of nails. Water stood to the third lintel exactly as he had promised. The sick went over the boards first, Sathen walking beside them with his medicines held against his chest and his rolled sleeves dark with rain. The congregation followed, and the old woman on Odrin's back turned her face up to the falling water as if she had never felt anything so clean.

The quay at the head of the Flats was a drowned mirror. Rain pounded the stone, ran off the mooring posts, dragged the ash in long gray ribbons out across the harbor. The quarter came up out of the dark behind them, out of the salt-dark passage, out of the tide that had stood to the third lintel and then fallen away like a hand letting go — fish-sellers, mothers, the hoop-boy, the branded whalers under their oilskins, the ones who could not walk still carried. Pella came out holding her lantern high in one hand and her oilcloth bundle under the other arm, and she did not let go of Voss's hand until she was sure the sky was over her instead of the stone.

Across the water, the Spire of Charters burned against the dawn. The rain could not reach it. The aerie's ring of windows glowed like a crown of coals, and even as they watched, the last of it gave way — the great folded weight coming down into itself with a sound that crossed the harbor like a name being crossed out. The ledgers, the leases, the iron letter's authors, the fire they had commissioned eating the hand that signed for it. The smoke went up straight and black into a sky the same color it had been over Gullrot.

Voss stood at the edge of the quay and watched that fire die against that sky, and he felt the faces in the smoke come and stand with him. The girl with the broken doll. The baker with his flour-dusted face. The crier whose voice his fire had silenced. The rest of them, the ones he had never let himself name. They were not angry. That was the terrible part. They simply stood, patient as tide, and he knew they would stand with him every night for the rest of his life, and that he would deserve them every night. He had stopped watching. He had not stopped being watched.

"Rain," Sathen said beside him, quiet, his breath a small white cloud in the cold. "Veyra's first honest rain in years. The city will say it was always going to rain, that the fire would have drowned anyway." He did not look at Voss. "Let them say it. The deep knows what happened."

The congregation was gathering itself on the quay, counting heads, the way a people who had moved through the dark count their own. Odrin moved among them with the old woman settled on the chapel steps, and his voice went up and down the crowd like a wave checking a shore. Children were crying; children were laughing; the hoop-boy had found a stick and was beating the puddles into spray. Iskra stood apart at the tide-wall, looking back across the harbor at what was left of the headland, her tarred coat streaming.

Then a voice cut the rain from the far quay, thin with distance and ragged with smoke.

"Burn-man! Voss!"

The woman magistrate stood at the water's edge across the channel, the ledger-keeper beside her clutching his branded palm, a handful of enforcers behind them who had worked their way around the fire-line. Her dress was scorched to the knee; her hair had come unbound; she pointed across the water with a hand that shook. "You drew our death! You will hang for it — the whole city will see it!"

The congregation turned. A hundred faces turned, and Voss felt them look at him and then look past him at the screaming woman, and something passed through them like a wind over water. No one moved aside. No one handed him over. The fish-seller who had once steadied his shoulder on the day of the chase stepped to stand nearer him. The woman who had brought him water did the same. Sathen went on standing beside him. Iskra walked over, slow, and stood at his shoulder, her knife still sheathed but her hand resting on its hilt, facing the far quay.

"Go back to your ash," she called across the water, her voice flat and tarred and carrying. "The quarter's not yours to cull tonight. The burn-man's not yours to hang. He's ours."

The magistrate's mouth worked. The rain swallowed whatever else she said. For a long moment she stood there, a burned woman on a burned quay with her burned world behind her, and then she turned and walked back toward the city, the ledger-keeper limping after her, and the enforcers folding around them like a shroud. The pursuit was not over. It would never be over. The whole city had been taught for fifteen years to hate the burn-man, and now the burn-man had burned the city's masters, and the story the city told about him would be a thing of knives. Voss knew this the way he knew tide tables: exactly, and too late to matter.

"No thanks," Iskra said, not looking at him. "I don't owe you thanks. You owed us the fire going where it went, and it went there, and now we're even, burn-man. But I've a boat that runs north before the spring watch, and I run it with people who need running. I'll have a place at the bow for a man who can read a coast like a ledger and draw what he sees." She finally looked at him, her eyes the color of harbor water in the rain. "Map the hidden places for me, cartographer. The ones where power would burn the innocent and call it justice. We'll go there first."

Voss opened his mouth. The faces in the smoke were standing all around him, patient, and he did not know if they were there to hold him or to be carried by him at last. He had been dead a long time; he had told the magistrate so. But the rain was on his face, and the children were laughing at the tide-wall, and Iskra was offering him a bow and a purpose, and for the first time in fifteen years the map he wanted to draw was not of a fire.

Then Pella was in front of him, holding out the oilcloth bundle, unwrapping it with the grave arithmetic of a girl who kept a ledger of prices and knew the cost of everything. Inside was a doll. Its paint flaked like ash. Its arm hung loose from the shoulder, and its face had been worn smooth by years of small hands. The Gullrot doll had burned in his fire, held up to his tower by a girl he never asked the name of. This one had come out of the Flats alive, and Pella held it out to him like a question.

"Will you stay?" she asked.

Voss looked at the fire across the harbor, dying against the same sky that had once seen Gullrot burn. Then he looked at the living children, at Pella's hoarse bright face, at the doll with its loose arm and flaking paint. The faces in the smoke waited. He had no words that would not sound like an excuse, and he had had enough of words that sounded like mercy when they were lines drawn around things he meant to burn.

He knelt in the rain on the washed stone of the quay, and he took the doll from her hands.

"Have you a needle and thread?" he asked.

Pella looked at him a long moment. Then she reached into her belt, past the ledger, and put a needle and a length of waxed thread into his hand, and stood over him while he worked, and the rain fell, and behind them across the harbor the last of the Spire of Charters settled into its own ash, and the people of the Drowned Flats came up out of the dark into the gray light of the first honest morning, and the burn-man knelt among them and mended, and did not watch the fire anymore.

set.name: Emmerich Voss
set.description: The Ignition Man, the Butcher of Gullrot, the burn-man; now a just arsonist and the one who carried the Drowned Flats out of the dark. Location: the rain-washed quay at the head of the Flats at dawn, having emerged from the salt-dark passage through the sunken door with the whole quarter; the Spire of Charters has collapsed into its own ash across the harbor. Physical/emotional condition: the god-thrill is spent; the rain is on his face; the faces in the smoke (the broken-doll girl, the baker, the crier, all the unnamed dead) stand with him and will come every night, and he accepts he deserves them. He knelt in the rain and mended Pella's doll with her needle and thread, his first honest act, and answered that he will stay. Knowledge/possessions: official fire plan burned with the Chantry; rewire executed; the folded tidal-iron survey and the iron letter still on his person (in his shoe); the second human chart and the vaults' fire geometry in his mind. Standing: the congregation of the deep closed around him and did not hand him over; Iskra claimed him ('the burn-man's not yours to hang. He's ours') and offered him a place at the bow of her smuggling boat running north before the spring watch, to map the hidden places where power would burn the innocent and guide people to safety. Goal: stay among the people he once meant to burn, mend what he can, map the hidden places for those who need running, and face the city's inevitable knives — the magistrate swore the whole city will hang him, and the pursuit remains live.

set.name: Chantry of the Deep Ledger
set.description: Secret tribunal of whaling magnates and maritime magistrates. Location/state: the Spire of Charters collapsed into itself at dawn — the aerie's ring of windows, the ledgers, the tidal-iron lease, and the iron letter's authors consumed by their own accelerant; the dry-dock warehouses and the Chantry's own quay are ash, drowned by rain that came too late to save them. Survivors: the woman magistrate and the ledger-keeper (brass key branded into his palm) survived and confronted the survivors from the far quay; the magistrate screamed that Voss drew their death and will hang, but was turned back by Iskra's claim and the congregation's wall of silence, walking away with her enforcers into the city. The pursuit is not over: the city has been taught for fifteen years to hate the burn-man, and the story it will tell is a thing of knives; her fate, pursuit, and the city's reckoning remain unresolved.

set.name: Iskra Venn
set.description: Smuggler captain of the Drowned Flats, tall, coarse salt-and-black hair in a rope, tarred coat over fisherman's jersey. Location: the rain-washed quay at dawn, having led the quarter through the tunnels and sunken door; she stood at Voss's shoulder facing the far quay when the magistrate came, and her knife stayed sheathed. State: she gives no thanks — 'I don't owe you thanks. You owed us the fire going where it went' — declaring them even, and claimed him from the magistrate ('the burn-man's not yours to hang. He's ours'). She offered Voss a place at the bow of her boat running north before the spring watch, for a man who can read a coast like a ledger and map the hidden places where power would burn the innocent; her trust rests on the fire having gone where it was owed. Goal: run the boat north with the people who need running, carrying the burn-man as her cartographer, and keep the quarter alive.

set.name: Brother Sathen
set.description: Heretic physician of the Drowned Flats, small and gray-haired, sleeves rolled, forearms stained by salt, chalk, and medicine. Location: the rain-washed quay at dawn with his patients and medicines, having brought the sick through the sunken door over the boards. State: he stood beside Voss through the magistrate's curse and said quietly that Veyra will claim the rain always would have come — 'Let them say it. The deep knows what happened.' He knows Voss is the burn-man who chose their lives and says nothing more of it. Goal: keep his sick, his branded, and his broken alive and see the quarter safe in the light.

set.name: Mael Odrin
set.description: Preacher of the congregation of the deep, tall and weathered, voice a low roll like a distant wave. Location: the rain-washed quay at dawn, the old woman settled on the chapel steps, moving among the congregation counting heads like a wave checking a shore. State: he heard the confession in the tunnels and said nothing; on the quay his presence and the congregation's wall of silence helped turn back the magistrate. Goal: hold the congregation together as one people and keep them alive in the new morning.

set.name: Pella
set.description: Scrappy fish-selling child of the Drowned Flats, about ten and a half, hoarse-voiced crier of 'Salt eel, three for a penny'; keeps a ledger of prices. Location: the rain-washed quay at dawn, her pierced-tin lantern and mended net and ledger with her, having come up out of the dark holding Voss's hand until the sky was over her. State: she named the burn-man in the tunnels and then claimed him as the one who carried them; on the quay she unwrapped her oilcloth bundle to reveal a doll whose paint flakes like ash and whose arm hangs loose — the living counterpart to the Gullrot doll that burned — and asked 'Will you stay?' He answered by kneeling and mending it with her needle and thread. Goal: keep hold of the burn-man who carried them, and see that he stays.

At dawn on the rain-washed quay at the head of the Flats, the whole quarter emerged from the salt-dark passage through the sunken door, the tide having stood to the third lintel exactly as Voss promised then fallen away; the sick crossed first over the boards, Sathen with his medicines, Odrin carrying the old woman, Pella holding Voss's hand until the sky was over them. The Spire of Charters collapsed into itself across the harbor, its aerie's ring of windows glowing like a crown of coals, its ledgers, leases, and the iron letter's authors consumed by their own accelerant; Voss watched that fire die against the same sky that once saw Gullrot burn.

The woman magistrate and the ledger-keeper (branded palm) reached the far quay with enforcers who had worked around the fire-line and screamed across the water that Voss drew their death and will hang before the whole city. The congregation did not hand him over: the fish-seller who steadied him, the woman who brought him water, and Sathen and Iskra closed around him, and Iskra called back 'The quarter's not yours to cull tonight. The burn-man's not yours to hang. He's ours.' The magistrate turned and walked back toward the city; her pursuit and the city's story remain live.

On the quay Iskra told Voss she owes him no thanks — he owed the quarter the fire going where it went, and now they are even — and offered him a place at the bow of her boat running north before the spring watch, to map the hidden places where power would burn the innocent and guide people to safety; he accepted by staying.

Pella unwrapped an oilcloth bundle on the quay to reveal a doll whose paint flaked like ash and whose arm hung loose — the living counterpart to the Gullrot doll that burned in Voss's fire — and asked 'Will you stay?' Voss answered with his first honest act: he knelt in the rain, took her needle and thread from her belt, and mended the doll while the rain fell and the Spire settled into ash behind them, closing the novel with his choice of what is worth burning for.

The woman magistrate survived and swore before the whole quay that the city will hang Voss; she turned back into the city with her enforcers and the ledger-keeper. The city has been taught for fifteen years to hate the burn-man, and the story it will tell is a thing of knives; her pursuit, her political survival, and the city's reckoning with the burn-man who burned its masters remain unresolved and may drive any continuation.

Iskra offered Voss a place at the bow of her smuggling boat running north before the spring watch, to map hidden places where power would burn the innocent and guide people to safety; he accepted by staying and kneeling to mend Pella's doll. His first run north with her, and what hidden places they map next, may drive any continuation.

Voss knows the faces in the smoke — the broken-doll girl, the baker, the crier, and all the unnamed dead of Gullrot — will stand with him every night for the rest of his life, and that he will deserve them every night; his redemption is a direction, not a clean slate, and his nightly reckoning with the dead continues.

errors.quote: Voss moved through the smoke with the map of the vaults fixed in his mind — he had drawn this building in the first days of his captivity, marking every load-bearing wall and tar-soaked post with an X, and the knowledge had never left him.
errors.pair: He did not draw fire-lines anymore. He had stopped after the night he woke to find he had sketched, without meaning to, the perfect ignition pattern for the Spire itself—every load-bearing wall, every tar-soaked post, with a small black X where the lever would go.
